skills.title: Turn an observation into a question that can be checked by testing
Make a prediction with a reason before testing
Describe the cycle of finding out: observe, question, predict, test, conclude, ask again

expectations: Science is a way of finding out by observing, asking questions and testing ideas, not just a list of facts to memorise.
A testable question can be answered by doing something and observing or measuring what happens (for example, does curd set faster in a warm place?).
A prediction is a guess with a reason, based on what we already know, made before the test; it can turn out wrong.
We test, observe carefully and record; the result either supports the prediction or does not, and it leads to new questions.
A prediction that turns out wrong is still useful because it teaches us something new.

misconceptions.belief: Science is a list of facts to memorise from a book, not a way of finding out.
signs: Says science means learning answers by heart
Asks 'which answer is right?' instead of 'how can we check?'
Thinks only scientists in labs can do science

diagnostic.prompt_en: Riya wants to know whether curd sets faster in a warm place. What is the most scientific way for her to find out?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Riya jaanna chahti hai ki kya garam jagah pe dahi jaldi jamta hai. Pata karne ka sabse 'scientist wala' tareeka kaunsa hai?

options.text: Read the answer somewhere and memorise it
Set two bowls of the same milk with the same starter, one in a warm place and one in a cool place, and check both after the same time
Ask one friend and believe whatever they say

remediation.representation: Two-bowl test card: warm bowl vs cool bowl, clock showing the same time for both
remediation.moveShape: Contrast 'look it up' with 'check it'; let the child design the two-bowl check and say what they would look for

misconceptions.belief: If a prediction turns out wrong, the experiment failed or was a waste.
signs: Changes the written prediction after seeing the result
Feels embarrassed when the result differs
Hides or ignores results that don't match

diagnostic.prompt_en: Aman predicted that his tulsi plant would grow better inside a dark cupboard. After two weeks it looked weak and pale. What should he think?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Aman ka guess tha ki tulsi ka paudha andhere cupboard mein zyada achha badhega. Do hafte baad paudha kamzor aur peela dikha. Ab Aman ko kya sochna chahiye?

options.text: My experiment failed; I should change my prediction to match
I learned something new: the plant seems to need light; I can ask why
Plants don't need anything at all

remediation.representation: Prediction log with a 'what I learned' column next to 'what happened'
remediation.moveShape: Celebrate a wrong prediction as a discovery; ask what new question it opens

misconceptions.belief: Every question can be answered by an experiment, including opinion questions.
signs: Tries to 'test' which cartoon or colour is best
Cannot tell an opinion question from a testable one

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which of these questions can be answered by doing a test?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inme se kaunsa sawaal test karke pata kiya ja sakta hai?

options.text: Which is the prettiest flower?
Does a wet cloth dry faster in the sun or in the shade?
Which festival is the most fun?

remediation.representation: Two baskets: 'I can check it by doing' vs 'It is someone's opinion'
remediation.moveShape: Sort a mix of questions together; child explains what they would do or measure for each testable one

items.prompt_en: Look around your kitchen. Turn one thing you notice into a question you could check by doing something.
items.prompt_hi: Apne kitchen mein dhyaan se dekho. Jo cheez notice karo, usse aisa sawaal banao jo tum kuch karke check kar sako.
items.answer: Any question that can be checked by trying something and observing, for example: 'Does sugar dissolve faster in warm water or cold water?'
acceptable: kya garam paani mein cheeni jaldi ghulti hai
does curd set faster in a warm place
does a wet tumbler dry faster near the window
hints: Invite them to name something in the kitchen that changes
Point to things that dissolve, dry, melt or set
Prompt: Does ___ happen faster when ___?
Assert: a testable question is one we can check by doing and watching

verified.solverAnswer: Any testable do-and-observe question, e.g. does sugar dissolve faster in warm water?

items.prompt_en: Predict first: will curd set faster in a warm place or in a cool place? Tell me why you think so.
items.prompt_hi: Pehle guess karo: dahi garam jagah pe jaldi jamega ya thandi jagah pe? Aur kyon lagta hai aisa?
items.answer: In the warm place; the tiny living things (bacteria) in the starter curd that turn milk into curd work faster in warmth, which is why curd takes longer to set in winter.
hints: Ask how long curd takes at home in summer and in winter
Point to what the spoon of old curd adds to the milk
Prompt: the tiny living things in curd work faster when it is ___
Assert: warm place; the curd bacteria work faster in warmth

verified.solverAnswer: Warm place, because warmth speeds up the bacteria that set curd (a guess I then test).

items.prompt_en: Meena puts one ice cube on a steel plate and wraps another ice cube in a woollen shawl. Predict which one will melt first.
items.prompt_hi: Meena ek ice cube steel ki plate pe rakhti hai aur doosra ek woollen shawl mein lapet deti hai. Guess karo, kaunsa pehle pighlega?
items.answer: The ice on the plate melts first. Wool does not make heat; it slows the room's warmth from reaching the ice, so the wrapped ice melts more slowly.
hints: Invite them to say what a shawl does for us in winter
Point to where the warmth is coming from in the room
Prompt: wool does not make heat; it only ___ heat moving through it
Assert: the plate ice melts first; wool slows warmth reaching the ice

verified.solverAnswer: The ice on the steel plate melts first; the woollen shawl insulates the wrapped one so it melts last.

items.prompt_en: You said curd sets faster in a warm place. How do you know? What is actually happening in the milk?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha garam jagah pe dahi jaldi jamta hai. Ye kaise pata? Doodh ke andar asal mein ho kya raha hai?
items.answer: The starter curd contains tiny living things (bacteria) that grow in the milk and turn it into curd; they grow and work faster when it is warm.
acceptable: jeevanu garmi mein tez kaam karte hain
hints: Ask why we add a spoon of old curd to the milk
Point to the starter as something alive
Prompt: the bacteria in the starter grow faster when it is ___
Assert: curd bacteria grow and work faster in warmth

verified.solverAnswer: Not yet known for sure; I only predicted. Warmth helps the bacteria in milk multiply and turn it to curd; test to check.

items.prompt_en: Meena had predicted the wrapped ice would melt first, but it melted last. Why is her test still good science?
items.prompt_hi: Meena ne socha tha ki shawl wali ice pehle pighlegi, par woh sabse baad mein pighli. Phir bhi uska test achhi science kyon hai?
items.answer: Because the test showed what really happens; a wrong prediction teaches us something new (wool slows heat) and leads to a new question. Science checks ideas instead of assuming them.
acceptable: galat guess se bhi seekhte hain
hints: Ask what Meena knows now that she didn't know before
Point to the new question her result raises
Prompt: a wrong prediction still teaches us ___
Assert: the test showed the truth; a wrong prediction is a discovery

verified.solverAnswer: A prediction can be wrong; the test still gave real evidence (wool keeps heat out/cold in) and she learned something.

items.prompt_en: Which question is testable: (A) 'Is mango the tastiest fruit?' or (B) 'Do mangoes ripen faster wrapped in newspaper or left in the open?' What makes the other one different?
items.prompt_hi: Kaunsa sawaal test kiya ja sakta hai: (A) 'Kya aam sabse tasty fruit hai?' ya (B) 'Kya aam newspaper mein lapetne se jaldi pakte hain ya khule mein rakhne se?' Doosra wala alag kyon hai?
items.answer: B is testable: we can wrap some mangoes, leave others open and watch which ripen first. A is an opinion; people can disagree and no test can settle it.
hints: Ask how they would check each question
Point to whether people could simply disagree about A
Prompt: we can check B by ___ and watching
Assert: B is testable; A is an opinion

verified.solverAnswer: B is testable; A is opinion/taste that no test can settle.

items.prompt_en: Rohan notices his tulsi plant leans towards the window. Using the steps of science, what question can he ask, what might he predict, and how could he test it?
items.prompt_hi: Rohan dekhta hai ki uska tulsi ka paudha khidki ki taraf jhuk raha hai. Science ke steps se batao: woh kya sawaal pooch sakta hai, kya guess kar sakta hai, aur test kaise karega?
items.answer: Question: does the plant bend towards light? Prediction: yes, it grows towards light. Test: turn the pot around so the plant leans away from the window and watch for a few days; it bends towards the window again.
hints: Invite them to say what is special about the window side
Point to turning the pot as a way to check
Prompt: if we turn the pot, I predict the plant will ___
Assert: ask, predict 'towards light', turn the pot, observe it bend back

verified.solverAnswer: Question: why does the plant lean to the window? Predict: leans toward light. Test: turn the pot around / put in a dark spot and watch over days.

items.prompt_en: Your mother says jaggery (gur) becomes soft and sticky in the rainy season. How could you check, like a scientist, whether damp air is the reason?
items.prompt_hi: Mummy kehti hain ki baarish ke mausam mein gur naram aur chipchipa ho jaata hai. Scientist ki tarah kaise check karoge ki kya nami wali hawa iski wajah hai?
items.answer: Take two similar pieces of jaggery; keep one in a closed dry jar and one in an open bowl in the same room for a few days; only the damp air differs. If only the open piece becomes sticky, damp air is the likely reason.
acceptable: ek band dabbe mein ek khula
two pieces, one closed one open
hints: Ask what is different about air in the rainy season
Point to making two pieces where only one thing differs
Prompt: one piece in a ___ jar and one in an ___ bowl, same room
Assert: closed vs open, everything else the same, then compare

verified.solverAnswer: Keep jaggery in a dry sealed jar and in damp air, same amount, compare after some days.

items.prompt_en: Put these steps of finding out in order and draw them as a circle: test, observe, predict, ask a question, conclude.
items.prompt_hi: In steps ko sahi order mein lagao aur ek circle mein draw karo: test, observe, predict, sawaal poochho, conclude.
items.answer: Observe → ask a question → predict → test → conclude → (new question, back to observing). It is a circle because each answer leads to new questions.
hints: Invite them to start with what comes first: noticing something
Point to the guess coming before the test
Prompt: observe, ask, ___, test, ___
Assert: observe, question, predict, test, conclude, and round again

verified.solverAnswer: Ask a question, predict, test, observe, conclude (and cycle again).
verified.note: Solver ordered ask-predict-test-observe-conclude; the key puts 'observe' first. Prompt lists 'observe' once, so the position of observe is ambiguous; key's own acceptable list is the same ordering. Reword prompt (e.g. 'notice something' as the first step) or accept both.

items.prompt_en: Golu says: 'I predicted the curd would set in the fridge. It didn't, so I'll write in my notebook that I predicted it wouldn't.' What is wrong with this?
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Mera guess tha ki fridge mein dahi jam jaayega. Nahi jama, toh main notebook mein likh doonga ki mera guess tha ki nahi jamega.' Isme galti kya hai?
items.answer: A prediction must be written before the test and never changed afterwards; changing it hides what he learned. A wrong prediction is useful information.
hints: Ask why we write the prediction before the test
Point to what Golu actually learned about the cold
Prompt: a prediction is written ___ the test and never ___
Assert: never change a prediction afterwards; the wrong guess is the lesson

verified.solverAnswer: He changed his prediction after seeing the result; predictions are written before and kept, then compared with result.

items.prompt_en: Your younger cousin thinks science means memorising answers. Explain to her how a scientist finds something out, using the curd example.
items.prompt_hi: Tumhari chhoti cousin sochti hai ki science matlab answers ratna. Use dahi wale example se samjhao ki scientist kaise koi baat pata karta hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: notice something (curd sets slowly in winter), ask a testable question, predict with a reason, test fairly (two bowls, warm and cool, same milk and starter, same time), observe and record, conclude, and ask the next question.
hints: Invite them to begin with what they noticed about curd
Point to the two-bowl test
Prompt: first we ask, then we ___, then we ___ it
Assert: science is finding out: ask, predict, test, observe, conclude

verified.solverAnswer: Ask a question, predict, test fairly with warm vs cool bowls, observe, conclude, never just memorise.

items.prompt_en: From our last lesson, without looking back: what is the difference between a random guess and a prediction in science?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar ki baat, bina dekhe batao: science mein random guess aur prediction mein kya farak hai?
items.answer: A prediction is a guess with a reason, based on what you already know, made before testing; a random guess has no reason behind it.
hints: Ask what they did before the ice-in-shawl test
Point to the 'because' part of a prediction
Prompt: a prediction is a guess with a ___
Assert: a prediction is a reasoned guess made before testing

verified.solverAnswer: A guess has no reasoning behind it; a prediction is based on what we know and is tested.

items.prompt_en: Before starting, Riya writes: 'I think the bowl in the warm place will set first.' Which step of science is this?
items.prompt_hi: Shuru karne se pehle Riya likhti hai: 'Mujhe lagta hai garam jagah wala katora pehle jamega.' Ye science ka kaunsa step hai?
items.answer: Making a prediction.
hints: Ask whether the test has started yet
Point to the words 'I think ... will'
Prompt: saying what you think will happen is called ___
Assert: that is the prediction step

verified.solverAnswer: Predicting (hypothesis step).

workedExample.problem: Does curd set faster in a warm place?
steps: Observe: at home, curd takes longer to set in winter than in summer
Ask a testable question: does curd set faster in a warm place than a cool one?
Predict with a reason: the warm bowl will set first because curd bacteria work faster in warmth
Test fairly: two bowls with the same milk, same amount and same spoon of starter; one in a warm spot, one in a cool spot
Observe and conclude: check both after the same time, record what you see, and say whether the prediction was supported
fadedVersion: Observe: at home, curd takes longer to set in ___
Ask a testable question: does curd set faster in a ___ place?
Predict with a reason: the warm bowl will set first because ___
Test fairly: two bowls with the same ___, same amount and same starter; one ___, one cool
Observe and conclude: check both after the ___ time and record

skills.title: Record observations in a table with clear headings and units
Identify what to change, what to keep the same, and what to observe or measure
Explain why only one thing changes in a fair test and why tests are repeated

expectations: In a fair test only one thing (the thing being tested) is changed; everything else is kept the same.
If many things change at once, we cannot tell which one caused the result.
We decide what to observe or measure and record it in a table with clear headings and units.
Observations are what we see or measure (dry after 30 minutes), not opinions (the cloth is nice).
Repeating a test makes the result more trustworthy.

misconceptions.belief: Changing many things at once gives a quicker answer.
signs: Plans cotton in the sun and nylon in the shade in the same test
Says 'it will be faster to change everything together'
Cannot say which change caused the result

diagnostic.prompt_en: Asha wants to know which cloth dries fastest. Which plan is fair?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Asha jaanna chahti hai ki kaunsa kapda sabse jaldi sookhta hai. Kaunsa plan fair hai?

options.text: Cotton in the sun, nylon in the shade and wool inside the room, all at once to save time
Same-size pieces of cotton, nylon and wool, each wetted with the same amount of water, hung side by side on the same line
A big cotton bedsheet and a small nylon hanky on the same line

remediation.representation: Fair-test planner card with three boxes: change / keep the same / measure
remediation.moveShape: Child fills the planner for an unfair plan, spots the second change, then fixes it

misconceptions.belief: One try is enough to be sure of a result.
signs: Stops after one result
Ignores an odd result
Says 'ho gaya, pata chal gaya'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Kabir tested two kinds of seeds once and the result surprised him. What should he do next?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kabir ne do tarah ke beej sirf ek baar test kiye aur result se hairaan ho gaya. Ab use kya karna chahiye?

options.text: Accept it; one test is enough
Repeat the test a few times the same way and see if the result stays the same
Change the seeds and the place together and test again

remediation.representation: Three-trial table where one trial is an odd result
remediation.moveShape: Show a three-trial table with one odd value; ask which result to trust and why repeating helped

misconceptions.belief: A record can be an opinion or a vague word instead of an observation or measurement.
signs: Writes 'cotton was nice' or 'nylon good'
Records 'wet' or 'dry' without time or units
Makes a table without headings

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which one is an observation you can record in a table?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inme se kaunsa observation hai jo table mein likha ja sakta hai?

options.text: The cotton cloth was dry after 40 minutes
Cotton is the best cloth
I like the nylon one

remediation.representation: Two-column sort: 'I saw or measured it' vs 'I feel or think it'
remediation.moveShape: Turn two opinion lines into measured observations together, then the child turns a third alone

items.prompt_en: In the cloth-drying test, what is the one thing you change? Name two things you keep the same.
items.prompt_hi: Kapda sukhane wale test mein kaunsi ek cheez badalte ho? Do cheezein batao jo same rakhte ho.
items.answer: Change only the type of cloth. Keep the same (any two): size of the cloth, amount of water, place and sunlight, time of hanging.
hints: Ask what the test is trying to find out
Point to the cloth types as the thing being compared
Prompt: we change only the ___, and keep the ___ and the ___ the same
Assert: change only the cloth type; keep size, water and place the same

verified.solverAnswer: Change the type of cloth; keep same size, same water amount, same place/time.

items.prompt_en: Make a table for the cloth test. What headings will your columns have?
items.prompt_hi: Cloth test ke liye ek table banao. Columns ki headings kya hongi?
items.answer: Type of cloth | Time taken to dry (minutes); a notes column is optional.
acceptable: type of cloth, time in minutes
hints: Ask what they will write for each cloth
Point to the unit for time
Prompt: one column for the ___ and one for the ___ in minutes
Assert: Type of cloth | Time to dry (minutes)

verified.solverAnswer: Type of cloth | time to dry (minutes) | maybe observations.

items.prompt_en: Predict: the same wet hanky is hung once spread open and once folded into four, in the same place. Which way will it dry faster?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: wahi geela rumaal ek baar khol ke failaya, ek baar chaar tah karke, same jagah pe. Kaise jaldi sookhega?
items.answer: Spread open; more of the cloth is open to the air, so the water evaporates faster. Only the folding changed, so this is a fair test.
hints: Invite them to picture how much cloth touches the air each way
Point to the inside folds that stay hidden
Prompt: more surface open to air means water leaves ___
Assert: spread open dries faster; only the folding changed

verified.solverAnswer: Spread open dries faster (more surface exposed).

items.prompt_en: Asha hangs cotton in the sun and nylon in the shade, and the cotton dries first. Before she decides, predict: can she say cotton dries faster than nylon?
items.prompt_hi: Asha cotton dhoop mein aur nylon chhaon mein taangti hai, aur cotton pehle sookhta hai. Socho: kya woh keh sakti hai ki cotton nylon se jaldi sookhta hai?
items.answer: No. Two things changed (cloth type and sun or shade), so the cotton may have dried first because of the sun. The test is unfair.
hints: Ask what was different about the two cloths besides the material
Point to the sun and shade
Prompt: two things changed, so we can't tell if it was the ___ or the ___
Assert: no conclusion; she changed two things

verified.solverAnswer: No; two things (cloth and place) differ so test is unfair.
verified.note: Agrees. Hint 2 names sun and shade, which is the reason itself.

items.prompt_en: Why must we change only one thing at a time in a fair test?
items.prompt_hi: Fair test mein ek baar mein sirf ek hi cheez kyon badalte hain?
items.answer: So that if the result changes, we know it was caused by that one thing; if many things change, we cannot tell which one caused it.
acceptable: pata chale kis wajah se hua
hints: Ask what Asha could not tell in her cloth test
Point to the two changes she made
Prompt: if only one thing changes, the result must be because of ___
Assert: one change means we know the cause

verified.solverAnswer: So that we know which one change caused the result.

items.prompt_en: Plan A: three same-size cloths, same water, hung together in the sun. Plan B: three different-size cloths, one in sun, one in shade, one under a fan. Which plan fairly tests the type of cloth, and what makes the other unfair?
items.prompt_hi: Plan A: teen same size ke kapde, same paani, saath mein dhoop mein. Plan B: teen alag size ke kapde, ek dhoop, ek chhaon, ek pankhe ke neeche. Kaunsa plan kapde ke type ka fair test hai, aur doosra unfair kyon hai?
items.answer: Plan A is fair. Plan B changes the size and the place as well as the cloth type, so we can't tell what caused any difference.
hints: Ask them to count how many things change in each plan
Point to size and place in Plan B
Prompt: Plan B changes the cloth, the ___ and the ___
Assert: A is fair; B changes three things

verified.solverAnswer: Plan A is fair; B changes size and place so unfair.

items.prompt_en: Kabir's record says: 'Cotton - fast. Nylon - good. Wool - I don't like it.' What is wrong with this record?
items.prompt_hi: Kabir ki notebook mein likha hai: 'Cotton - fast. Nylon - achha. Wool - mujhe pasand nahi.' Is record mein kya gadbad hai?
items.answer: These are opinions and vague words, not observations; he should record a measurement for each cloth, such as time taken to dry in minutes, under clear headings.
hints: Ask what 'fast' and 'good' tell someone reading it later
Point to the clock as the thing to read
Prompt: instead of 'fast', write the ___ in minutes
Assert: record measurements like minutes to dry, not likes or dislikes

verified.solverAnswer: Not measured or recorded as observations; opinions/vague words instead of numbers like time.

items.prompt_en: You want to find out whether a cricket ball bounces higher on a concrete floor or on grass. How do you make it a fair test?
items.prompt_hi: Tum jaanna chahte ho ki cricket ball cement ke farsh pe zyada uchhalti hai ya ghaas pe. Ise fair test kaise banaoge?
items.answer: Use the same ball, drop it (don't throw it) from the same height each time, measure the bounce height on each surface, change only the surface, and repeat a few times.
hints: Ask what could accidentally make one bounce higher
Point to throwing versus dropping
Prompt: same ball, same ___, only the ___ changes
Assert: same ball, same height, drop it, only the surface changes, repeat

verified.solverAnswer: Same ball, same drop height, same way of dropping; change only the surface; measure bounce height; repeat.

items.prompt_en: A farmer says his new fertiliser made his wheat grow taller this year. But this year also had more rain. Can he be sure? How could he test it fairly?
items.prompt_hi: Ek kisaan kehta hai ki naye khaad se iss saal uska gehun lamba hua. Par iss saal baarish bhi zyada hui. Kya woh pakka keh sakta hai? Fair test kaise karega?
items.answer: He can't be sure, because two things changed (fertiliser and rain). Fair test: two similar plots in the same field, same seeds, same water and care in the same season, fertiliser on only one plot; then compare.
hints: Ask what else was different this year
Point to rain as a second change
Prompt: two plots in the same season, fertiliser on ___ one only
Assert: not sure; compare two plots where only fertiliser differs

verified.solverAnswer: No, rain is another changed factor. Grow plots with and without fertiliser, same wheat, soil, water, sun.

items.prompt_en: Riya's notes say: 'The cotton hanky dried in 30 minutes, the nylon one in 20 minutes, and the woollen one took 50 minutes.' Put this in a table and tell me which dried fastest.
items.prompt_hi: Riya ke notes: 'Cotton rumaal 30 minute mein sookha, nylon 20 minute mein, aur woollen wala 50 minute mein.' Ise table mein likho aur batao sabse jaldi kaunsa sookha.
items.answer: Table: Cloth | Time to dry (min): Cotton 30, Nylon 20, Wool 50. Nylon dried fastest.
hints: Invite them to draw two columns first
Point to the smallest number of minutes
Prompt: the fewest minutes means it dried ___
Assert: nylon, 20 minutes, dried fastest

verified.solverAnswer: Table cloth vs time; nylon fastest (20 min).

items.prompt_en: Why do scientists repeat a test instead of doing it just once?
items.prompt_hi: Scientist ek test sirf ek baar karne ki jagah baar-baar kyon karte hain?
items.answer: One result can be a mistake or happen by chance; repeating checks that the result stays the same, so it can be trusted.
acceptable: to check it is not by chance
hints: Ask what could go wrong in a single try
Point to Kabir's surprising result
Prompt: if the result is the same every time, we can ___ it
Assert: repeating rules out mistakes and chance

verified.solverAnswer: One result could be a fluke; repeating checks it is reliable.

items.prompt_en: Teach your friend how to plan a fair test to find which soap makes the most foam. Tell her what to change, what to keep the same and what to record.
items.prompt_hi: Apni dost ko sikhao ki kaunsa sabun sabse zyada jhaag banata hai, iska fair test kaise plan kare. Batao kya badalna hai, kya same rakhna hai aur kya likhna hai.
items.answer: Change only the type of soap. Keep the same: amount of soap, amount of water, same bottle, same number of shakes. Record the height of the foam (in cm) for each soap in a table, and repeat.
hints: Invite them to start with the one thing that changes
Point to the shaking and the amount of water
Prompt: change only the ___, keep ___ the same, measure the foam ___
Assert: one soap change; same water, amount and shakes; record foam height; repeat

verified.solverAnswer: Change soap type; keep same water amount, same stirring, same container; record foam height.

items.prompt_en: From our last lesson: in a fair test, how many things do we change on purpose at a time?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhle lesson se: fair test mein ek baar mein jaan-boojh kar kitni cheezein badalte hain?
items.answer: Only one; everything else is kept the same.
hints: Ask them to recall the cloth-drying plan
Point to what changed in that plan
Prompt: we change only ___ thing
Assert: only one thing changes

verified.solverAnswer: One.

workedExample.problem: Which cloth dries fastest: cotton, nylon or wool?
steps: Decide what to change: only the type of cloth
Keep the rest the same: same-size pieces, same amount of water, hung side by side at the same time
Decide what to measure: time until each piece is dry, checking every 10 minutes
Record in a table with headings: Cloth | Time to dry (minutes)
Repeat the test, compare the times and conclude which cloth dried fastest
fadedVersion: Decide what to change: only the ___
Keep the rest the same: same-size pieces, same amount of ___, hung side by side
Decide what to measure: ___ until each piece is dry
Record in a table with headings: ___ | ___
___ the test, compare and conclude

skills.title: Tell a soft green stem from a hard woody stem
Classify a plant as herb, shrub or tree using stem type and where branches start
Recognise climbers and creepers as plants with weak stems

expectations: Plants are grouped by their stems: herbs have soft green stems; shrubs have hard woody stems that branch out near the ground; trees have one thick hard woody main stem (trunk) with branches higher up.
Height alone does not decide the group: a young mango sapling is still a tree, and a tall banana plant is a herb because its stem is soft, not woody.
Herbs are usually short, shrubs medium-sized and trees tall, but the stem is the real test.
Plants with weak stems that cannot stand upright either climb on a support (climbers like money plant and bottle gourd) or spread along the ground (creepers like pumpkin and watermelon).

skills.title: Identify reticulate (net-like) and parallel venation in leaves
Identify tap roots and fibrous roots

expectations: Veins in a leaf form a pattern: reticulate venation is a net-like pattern (mango, tulsi, hibiscus); parallel venation has veins running side by side (grass, wheat, maize, banana).
A tap root has one main thick root with smaller side roots (mustard, mango, carrot, radish); fibrous roots are many thin roots of similar size growing from the base of the stem (grass, wheat, onion).
Plants with reticulate venation usually have tap roots; plants with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots.
So by looking at a leaf we can usually predict the root type without digging up the plant.

skills.title: Say what a habitat is and name habitats such as desert, cold mountains and water
Link a body feature of a plant or animal to how it helps survival in its habitat

expectations: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives and gets food, water, shelter and suitable conditions.
Adaptations are special features that help an organism survive in its habitat, e.g. a camel's long legs and wide padded feet for hot sand, a yak's long thick hair for the cold.
Desert plants like cactus have spines instead of broad leaves, thick fleshy stems that store water and a waxy coat, all reducing water loss.
Water plants and animals have features for water: fish have gills, fins and a streamlined body; lotus has floating leaves with a waxy, water-repelling surface.
Adaptations are not chosen by an animal during its life; they develop over a very long time, over many generations.

items.prompt_en: What is a habitat? Name the habitat of a camel, a yak and a fish.
items.prompt_hi: Habitat kya hota hai? Oont, yak aur machhli ka habitat batao.
items.answer: A habitat is the place where a living thing lives and gets food, water and shelter. Camel: desert (like the Thar); yak: cold mountains (like Ladakh); fish: water (rivers, ponds, sea).
hints: Ask where each animal is usually seen
Point to what each place gives the animal
Prompt: a habitat is where an animal ___ and gets food and ___
Assert: home with food, water, shelter; desert, cold mountains, water

verified.solverAnswer: Habitat: the place where a living thing lives. Camel desert; yak mountains/cold; fish water.

items.prompt_en: Name two features of a camel and say how each helps it live in the desert.
items.prompt_hi: Oont ki do khoobiyan batao aur har ek registaan mein kaise madad karti hai.
items.answer: Any two: long legs keep its body away from the hot sand; wide padded feet don't sink into sand; it can go many days without drinking water; long eyelashes keep sand out of its eyes; it can close its nostrils against sand; its hump stores fat for energy.
hints: Invite them to picture a camel walking on hot sand
Point to the feet and the eyelashes
Prompt: wide padded feet stop it from ___ into the sand
Assert: e.g. long legs keep it off hot sand; padded feet stop sinking

verified.solverAnswer: Hump stores fat; long legs keep body away from hot sand; wide feet; long eyelashes against sand; water-saving.

items.prompt_en: Predict: a cactus and a money plant are both not watered for three weeks in a hot place. Which will still look healthy, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: cactus aur money plant dono ko garam jagah pe teen hafte paani nahi diya. Kaun sa abhi bhi theek dikhega, aur kyon?
items.answer: The cactus: its thick fleshy stem stores water, and spines instead of broad leaves and a waxy coat cut down water loss.
hints: Ask where cactus naturally grows
Point to its thick stem and spines
Prompt: a thick stem can ___ water and spines lose ___ water
Assert: cactus; it stores water and loses very little

verified.solverAnswer: Cactus; stores water in stem, thick waxy skin, spines reduce water loss.

items.prompt_en: A deodar or pine tree in the hills is shaped like a cone with sloping branches. Predict what happens to heavy snow falling on it, compared with a wide, flat-topped tree.
items.prompt_hi: Pahaadon ka deodar ya cheed ka ped cone jaisa hota hai, jhuki hui daaliyon wala. Guess karo, uspe bhaari barf giregi toh kya hoga, ek chaude sapaat chhat wale ped ke mukaable?
items.answer: Snow slides off the sloping branches of the cone-shaped tree, so the branches don't break; on a wide flat-topped tree snow piles up and branches can break.
hints: Invite them to picture snow on a sloping roof
Point to the downward slope of the branches
Prompt: on sloping branches, snow ___
Assert: snow slides off the cone; flat branches may break

verified.solverAnswer: Snow slides off the sloping conical branches; flat tree would hold snow and break.

items.prompt_en: Pour a few drops of water on a lotus leaf or an arbi (colocasia) leaf from the market. Predict what the water will do.
items.prompt_hi: Kamal ki patti ya bazaar se laayi arbi ki patti pe paani ki kuch boondein daalo. Guess karo, paani kya karega?
items.answer: The water forms round drops that roll off, because the leaf's surface is waxy and water-repelling; the leaf stays dry.
hints: Ask what happens to rain on a raincoat
Point to the shiny surface of the leaf
Prompt: a waxy surface makes water ___ off
Assert: drops roll off; the waxy leaf stays dry

verified.solverAnswer: Water beads up and rolls off.

items.prompt_en: Why can't a fish live on land, even if you give it plenty of food?
items.prompt_hi: Machhli ko kitna bhi khana do, woh zameen pe kyon nahi reh sakti?
items.answer: It breathes with gills, which take in oxygen dissolved in water; out of water its gills cannot work, so it cannot breathe. Its fins are for swimming, not walking.
acceptable: galphade paani mein kaam karte hain
hints: Ask how a fish breathes
Point to the gills
Prompt: gills take oxygen from ___
Assert: gills only work in water; food doesn't fix that

verified.solverAnswer: Fish breathes with gills in water; cannot get oxygen on land.

items.prompt_en: Compare a fish and a frog. Both can swim, but a frog can also live on land. What features let each do this?
items.prompt_hi: Machhli aur medhak compare karo. Dono tair sakte hain, par medhak zameen pe bhi reh sakta hai. Kaun si khoobiyan dono ko ye karne deti hain?
items.answer: Fish: gills, fins and a streamlined body, so it lives only in water. Frog: lungs (and moist skin) to breathe air, strong back legs for jumping and webbed feet for swimming, so it lives on land and in water.
hints: Invite them to start with how each breathes
Point to the frog's back legs and webbed feet
Prompt: fish breathes with ___, frog with ___
Assert: fish gills and fins; frog lungs, jumping legs, webbed feet

verified.solverAnswer: Fish: gills, fins, streamlined; frog: lungs and moist skin, webbed feet, legs for land.

items.prompt_en: A snow leopard lives high in the Himalayas. Guess two features it might have that help it there.
items.prompt_hi: Snow leopard Himalaya mein bahut oonchaai pe rehta hai. Do khoobiyan guess karo jo wahan uski madad karti hongi.
items.answer: Any two: thick fur for warmth; wide furry paws that work like snowshoes; a long thick tail to wrap around itself and for balance; colouring that blends with rocks and snow.
hints: Ask what is hardest about living in snow
Point to the yak's thick hair as a clue
Prompt: to stay warm it needs thick ___
Assert: thick fur and wide furry paws, for example

verified.solverAnswer: Thick fur, padded large paws, strong legs for climbing, camouflage.

items.prompt_en: In hot summers people in Delhi wear loose cotton clothes, and in Ladakh people wear thick woollen layers. How is this like an adaptation, and how is it different?
items.prompt_hi: Delhi mein garmi mein log dheele cotton ke kapde pehente hain, aur Ladakh mein moti woollen layers. Ye adaptation jaisa kaise hai, aur alag kaise?
items.answer: Like: it helps people cope with the conditions. Different: people choose and change clothes quickly, while an animal's adaptations are body features it is born with, which developed over many generations; it cannot take them off.
hints: Ask whether a yak can take off its hair in summer
Point to choosing versus being born with
Prompt: clothes are ___; an animal's features come over many ___
Assert: similar purpose; but clothes are a choice, adaptations are inherited over generations

verified.solverAnswer: Clothes are chosen by people and can change anytime; adaptation is an inherited body feature developed over many generations.

items.prompt_en: Draw a camel and label three features that help it in the desert, with a few words on how each helps.
items.prompt_hi: Ek oont banao aur teen khoobiyan label karo jo registaan mein madad karti hain, har ek ke saath kuch shabd ki kaise madad karti hai.
items.answer: Any three, e.g.: long legs, keep away from hot sand; padded feet, don't sink; long eyelashes, keep sand out; hump, stores fat.
hints: Invite them to label from the feet upwards
Point to the eyes and the hump
Prompt: hump stores ___, not water
Assert: legs, feet, eyelashes, hump, each with its job

verified.solverAnswer: Hump (fat), long legs, broad padded feet, long eyelashes, nostrils.

items.prompt_en: Golu says: 'The camel wanted to store water, so it grew a hump full of water.' Find the two mistakes.
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Oont paani jama karna chahta tha, isliye usne paani se bhara koohad uga liya.' Do galtiyan dhundho.
items.answer: 1) The hump stores fat, not water. 2) Animals don't grow features because they want them; adaptations developed over many generations.
hints: Ask what is really inside the hump
Point to the word 'wanted'
Prompt: the hump stores ___, and features come over many ___
Assert: fat not water; adaptations aren't chosen

verified.solverAnswer: Hump stores fat not water; camel didn't grow it by wanting - adaptation arises over generations.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your friend what an adaptation is, using one desert, one cold and one water example.
items.prompt_hi: Apne dost ko samjhao adaptation kya hota hai, ek registaan, ek thandi jagah aur ek paani ka example dekar.
items.answer: Key ideas: an adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat; desert: cactus spines and fleshy stem or camel's padded feet; cold: yak's thick hair or cone-shaped pine trees; water: fish gills and fins or lotus floating waxy leaves; adaptations developed over many generations.
hints: Invite them to define the word first
Point to one example per habitat
Prompt: an adaptation is a ___ that helps it ___ in its home
Assert: survival features, built over generations, with one example per habitat

verified.solverAnswer: Adaptation is a feature that helps survive in a habitat: camel hump fat, thick fur in cold, fins/gills in water.

items.prompt_en: From last time: what is the special word for features that help a living thing survive in its habitat?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: jo khoobiyan kisi jeev ko apne habitat mein jeene mein madad karti hain, unke liye khaas shabd kya hai?
items.answer: Adaptations.
hints: Ask them to recall the camel's padded feet
Point to 'features that fit the home'
Prompt: these features are called ___
Assert: adaptations

verified.solverAnswer: Adaptation.

workedExample.problem: Explain how a cactus is adapted to the desert.
steps: Name the habitat's challenge: very little water and a hot sun
Feature: spines instead of broad leaves, so less water is lost
Feature: a thick, fleshy green stem that stores water and makes food
Feature: a waxy coat that cuts water loss, and roots that spread wide to soak up rain quickly
Conclusion: each feature helps the cactus save or collect water
fadedVersion: Name the habitat's challenge: very little ___ and a hot sun
Feature: ___ instead of broad leaves, so less water is lost
Feature: a thick, fleshy stem that ___ water
Feature: a ___ coat that cuts water loss
Conclusion: each feature helps the cactus ___ or collect water

skills.title: Explain how living things depend on each other (food, pollination, seed spreading, clean-up)
Predict how losing one species affects others
Suggest ways to conserve diversity

expectations: Biodiversity means the variety of plants, animals and other living things in a place.
Living things depend on each other for food, pollination, spreading seeds and cleaning up dead matter, so losing one species affects many others.

In India, vultures fell sharply after eating carcasses of cattle treated with the painkiller diclofenac; with fewer vultures, carcasses lay rotting longer, stray dogs increased and the risk of diseases such as rabies rose.
Every species has a role, including small or 'unattractive' ones like earthworms, insects and vultures.
We conserve diversity by protecting habitats (forests, wetlands, sacred groves), avoiding pollution and harmful chemicals, not hunting wild animals and planting native species.

misconceptions.belief: Losing one species does not affect others.
signs: Says 'one bird less, what difference does it make?'
Cannot trace a chain of effects
Thinks only the lost species suffers

diagnostic.prompt_en: If honeybees disappeared from a mustard-growing area, what would happen?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Agar sarson ugane wale ilaake se madhumakkhiyan gayab ho jaayein, toh kya hoga?

options.text: Nothing much; bees only make honey
Fewer mustard flowers would be pollinated, so there would be fewer seeds and less mustard
Mustard plants would grow bigger because no bees disturb them

remediation.representation: Domino chain: bees → pollination → seeds → oil → farmer's income
remediation.moveShape: Remove one domino and let the child narrate each fall; then they build a chain for a new species

misconceptions.belief: Only big, useful or beautiful animals matter; creatures like vultures, earthworms and insects are useless.
signs: Calls vultures 'dirty and useless'
Wants all insects killed
Ranks animals by how cute they are

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which of these does the most to clean up dead animals lying in the open?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Khule mein pade mare hue jaanwaron ko saaf karne ka sabse zyada kaam inme se kaun karta hai?

options.text: Vultures
Peacocks
Nobody; dead animals simply disappear by themselves

remediation.representation: Job cards: 'nature's cleaner', 'soil maker', 'pollinator', each with an unpopular creature
remediation.moveShape: Child matches each 'ugly' creature to its job and says what goes wrong if the job stops

misconceptions.belief: Planting any trees, even one kind in rows, is as good as a natural forest for diversity.
signs: Equates a plantation of one tree type with a forest
Counts only the number of trees

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which place will have the most kinds of birds and insects?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kis jagah pe sabse zyada tarah ke pakshi aur keede honge?

options.text: A natural forest with many kinds of trees, shrubs and herbs
A plantation of 1000 trees of only one kind
A cement parking lot

remediation.representation: Two-panel picture: layered natural forest vs single-species rows, with homes and foods marked
remediation.moveShape: Count foods and homes in each panel together; child explains why variety supports more animals

items.prompt_en: Give one example of how plants and animals help each other.
items.prompt_hi: Ek example do ki paudhe aur jaanwar ek doosre ki madad kaise karte hain.
items.answer: Any one: bees carry pollen between flowers and get nectar; birds eat fruits and spread the seeds; trees give birds shelter; earthworms make the soil good for plants.
hints: Ask what a bee does at a flower
Point to what the flower gets back
Prompt: bees get nectar and flowers get ___
Assert: e.g. bees pollinate flowers while feeding on nectar

verified.solverAnswer: Bees pollinate flowers and get nectar.

items.prompt_en: What job does a vulture do in nature?
items.prompt_hi: Prakriti mein giddh kya kaam karta hai?
items.answer: It eats dead animals (carcasses), cleaning up the surroundings and reducing the spread of disease.
hints: Ask what happens to a dead cow left in a field
Point to who comes to eat it
Prompt: vultures eat ___ animals
Assert: vultures are nature's cleaners of carcasses

verified.solverAnswer: Eats dead animals, cleaning environment.

items.prompt_en: A village's frogs all disappear because their pond was filled with soil. Predict what happens to the insects there, and to the snakes that eat frogs.
items.prompt_hi: Ek gaon ka talaab mitti se bhar diya gaya aur saare medhak gayab ho gaye. Guess karo, wahan ke keedon ka kya hoga, aur medhak khaane wale saanpon ka?
items.answer: Insects that frogs eat, such as mosquitoes, may increase; snakes that eat frogs have less food and may become fewer or move away.
hints: Ask what frogs eat and who eats frogs
Point to the frog in the middle of the chain
Prompt: without frogs, insects ___ and snakes ___
Assert: insects may increase; snakes lose food

verified.solverAnswer: Insects increase; snakes decline or hunt other prey.

items.prompt_en: India lost most of its vultures. Predict what happened to dead cattle lying in the open, and to the number of stray dogs.
items.prompt_hi: Bharat mein zyada-tar giddh khatam ho gaye. Guess karo, khule mein pade mare hue jaanwaron ka kya hua, aur aawara kutton ki sankhya ka?
items.answer: Carcasses lay rotting for longer, and stray dogs fed on them, so the number of stray dogs went up, raising the risk of dog bites and rabies.
hints: Ask who else eats carcasses if vultures are gone
Point to more food for stray dogs
Prompt: more leftover carcasses meant more ___
Assert: carcasses rotted longer; stray dogs increased

verified.solverAnswer: Carcasses pile up and rot; stray dogs increase.

items.prompt_en: You said stray dogs increased when vultures declined. Why is that dangerous for people?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha giddh kam hue toh aawara kutte badh gaye. Ye logon ke liye khatarnaak kyon hai?
items.answer: More dogs means more dog bites, and dogs can spread rabies, a deadly disease; rotting carcasses also spread germs and smell.
hints: Ask what disease people fear from dog bites
Point to rotting carcasses as a second problem
Prompt: more dogs → more bites → more ___
Assert: rabies and germs; the loss of vultures harmed people too

verified.solverAnswer: Dogs feed on carcasses, increase, spread rabies and disease.

items.prompt_en: Compare a natural forest with a plantation of a single kind of tree. Which has more diversity, and why does that matter?
items.prompt_hi: Ek prakritik jungle aur sirf ek tarah ke pedon ka plantation compare karo. Kis mein zyada vividhta hai, aur ye kyon zaroori hai?
items.answer: The natural forest; its many kinds of plants give many kinds of food and homes for many animals, and if one species is lost, others can still keep the web going.
hints: Ask how many kinds of food each place offers
Point to the different layers in a forest
Prompt: more kinds of plants means more ___ and ___ for animals
Assert: the natural forest; variety supports more life

verified.solverAnswer: Natural forest has more diversity; healthier stable ecosystem, resists pests/disease.

items.prompt_en: In some places farmers sprayed so much insect poison that bees and butterflies became rare. What could happen to their fruit and vegetable crops?
items.prompt_hi: Kuch jagah kisaanon ne itna keetnaashak chhidka ki madhumakkhiyan aur titliyan bahut kam ho gayin. Unki phal aur sabzi ki fasal ka kya ho sakta hai?
items.answer: Fewer pollinators means fewer flowers are pollinated and become fruits, so the harvest of crops like mango, pumpkin and mustard falls.
hints: Ask what bees and butterflies do for flowers
Point to flower → fruit
Prompt: fewer pollinators means fewer ___ become fruits
Assert: harvests fall without pollinators

verified.solverAnswer: Less pollination, so lower fruit and vegetable yield.

items.prompt_en: Many Indian villages protect 'sacred groves' (devrai, devban, kavu) where nobody cuts trees. How does this help biodiversity?
items.prompt_hi: Bharat ke kai gaon 'sacred groves' (devrai, devban, kavu) bachate hain jahan koi ped nahi kaatta. Isse vividhta ko kaise madad milti hai?
items.answer: The grove keeps a patch of natural forest safe, so many native plants, birds, insects and other animals survive there; it also protects springs and acts as a source of seeds for the area.
hints: Ask what lives in an uncut patch of old forest
Point to the grove as a safe home
Prompt: no cutting means the ___ stays safe for many species
Assert: protected habitat keeps many species alive

verified.solverAnswer: Protects many plants, animals and habitat from cutting.

items.prompt_en: Turn this into a chain with arrows: grass is eaten by deer, and deer are eaten by tigers. Then tell me what happens to the tigers if the deer disappear.
items.prompt_hi: Isse teer wali chain mein badlo: ghaas ko hiran khaata hai, aur hiran ko baagh. Phir batao agar hiran gayab ho jaayein toh baaghon ka kya hoga.
items.answer: Grass → deer → tiger. Without deer, tigers lose their main food, so they go hungry, become fewer, move away or may attack village cattle.
hints: Invite them to draw the arrows in the direction of 'is eaten by'
Point to the middle link
Prompt: if the middle link goes, the tiger loses its ___
Assert: grass → deer → tiger; removing deer starves tigers

verified.solverAnswer: Grass -> deer -> tiger; tigers starve or decline.

items.prompt_en: Golu says: 'Earthworms and vultures are useless creatures. We should only protect tigers and peacocks.' What would you tell Golu?
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Kenchue aur giddh bekaar jeev hain. Hume sirf baagh aur mor bachane chahiye.' Tum Golu ko kya bataoge?
items.answer: Every species has a role: earthworms loosen soil and make it fertile; vultures clean up carcasses. Losing them harms other living things, including people.
hints: Ask what earthworms do in a garden
Point to the vulture story
Prompt: earthworms make soil ___ and vultures clean up ___
Assert: all species have roles; losing 'unattractive' ones hurts us too

verified.solverAnswer: Every creature has a role; vultures clean, earthworms enrich soil.

items.prompt_en: Explain the vulture story to your parents and what it teaches us about diversity.
items.prompt_hi: Apne mummy-papa ko giddh wali kahani samjhao aur batao isse vividhta ke baare mein kya seekh milti hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: cattle were given the painkiller diclofenac; vultures eating their carcasses died; carcasses rotted, stray dogs increased and rabies risk rose; lesson: species depend on each other, so losing one affects many, including humans; harmful chemicals must be stopped and species protected.
hints: Invite them to start with what killed the vultures
Point to the chain of effects after
Prompt: fewer vultures → more rotting carcasses → more ___ → more ___
Assert: one lost species set off a chain that reached people

verified.solverAnswer: Vulture decline led to rotting carcasses, dogs, disease; each species matters.

items.prompt_en: From last time: name two things people can do to protect the variety of living things around us.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: do kaam batao jo log apne aas-paas ki vividhta bachane ke liye kar sakte hain.
items.answer: Any two: protect forests and other habitats; don't pollute ponds and rivers; plant native trees; avoid harmful pesticides and drugs that poison wildlife; don't hunt or capture wild animals; keep water for birds in summer; protect sacred groves.
hints: Ask what harmed the vultures and the bees
Point to protecting homes of animals
Prompt: we can protect ___ and stop using harmful ___
Assert: e.g. protect habitats and avoid harmful chemicals

verified.solverAnswer: Plant trees, protect habitats, avoid pollution, no hunting.
